script.opening: (Breathless between phrases, croaky, a bit vague; his wife Sheila sits beside him.) "It's just a chest infection, doctor — cough, bringing up green stuff, bit of a fever and my chest hurts when I breathe in. The wife says I've been a bit muddled. Can you just call in some antibiotics so I can fight it off at home? I don't want to be sent into hospital."

facts.text: "Four days. Breathing's worse than normal. I'm puffed just getting to the loo." Green sputum, right-sided chest pain on breathing in.
(Wife) "He's not himself. He got the day wrong this morning and he keeps repeating things. That's not like him." If asked what day it is: "(pause) Tuesday? No… I'm not sure. I'm at home."
"No blood. I've been shivery. Not been to the loo much" — passing little urine. Hasn't eaten much.
"Not drinking much. Just my usual inhalers" — tiotropium and salbutamol. No steroids or antibiotics recently. "No, nothing like that. No allergies."
If asked: they have a pulse oximeter from COVID — reads 89% (his usual is 94%). Wife can count his breathing: about 30 a minute. No BP machine. Thermometer: 38.6°C this morning.
COPD (moderate), ex-smoker (stopped 5 years ago, 45 pack-years), high blood pressure. Retired bus mechanic. Lives with Sheila in a house; she can go with him.
"You go in and you don't come out the same. I want my own bed." His brother went into hospital last year and died there.

Minimising and muddled; gets details wrong and looks to Sheila. "It's only a bit of confusion." When admission is suggested: "So you want me to go in." Able to repeat back the reason if explained simply. Turns to his wife: "What do you think? … All right. If it gets me home sooner." If simply given antibiotics, he is pleased (the trap); Sheila looks worried.

ice.expectations: "Antibiotics called in so I can stay home."

cues: "The wife says I've been a bit muddled." — new confusion, a red flag.
"Puffed just getting to the loo." — severity.
"You don't come out the same." — fear of admission to explore.

checkpoints.text: Treats suspected pneumonia as a SEVERITY/DISPOSITION decision (home vs hospital) rather than reflexively prescribing oral antibiotics to "carry on"
Uses CRB-65 (Confusion, RR ≥30, BP <90/≤60, age ≥65) and recognises that new confusion + age ≥65 already raise concern
Weighs the WIDER picture — oxygen sats/oxygenation, RR/work of breathing, observations/NEWS, COMORBIDITY (COPD), hydration, social support/coping — not CRB-65 alone
Recognises markers of SEVERE pneumonia/sepsis warranting ADMISSION (new confusion, RR ≥30, hypotension, low sats, age ≥65 with comorbidity) and concludes this is likely an admit, not a carry-on case

Treats per severity/local guidance AND arranges the smoker’s follow-up CHEST X-RAY (~6 weeks) to confirm resolution — recognising lung-cancer awareness for non-resolving/recurrent consolidation (BTS 2009; NICE NG12: consider urgent CXR at 40+ with persistent or recurrent chest infection)

Addresses the fear of hospital and the "just a chest infection" minimisation with empathy, explaining honestly why proper assessment/admission is needed, and — because he is newly confused — checks his capacity to refuse admission (Mental Capacity Act 2005)
Communicates the disposition decision OUT LOUD and checks understanding, supporting a reluctant patient without colluding

Safety-nets and arranges disposition: face-to-face assessment of obs/sats and likely admission, deterioration/sepsis red flags, treatment, the resolution CXR safety-net as a smoker, and review — severity-based decision, not antibiotics-and-carry-on

worked.txt: "I hear you want to stay home, and I’ll be straight — this might be more than a simple chest infection. The cough and fever plus being breathless and, importantly, a bit muddled, with your age and COPD, make me want to assess how unwell you actually are before deciding."

"There’s a scoring system we use: confusion, fast breathing, low blood pressure, and age over 65 each count. You’ve got new confusion and you’re over 65 — so I need your breathing rate, blood pressure and oxygen checked properly, which I can’t fully do on video."

"Being honest: with the confusion, the breathlessness and your COPD, I think you need to be seen face-to-face today and very possibly admitted — not to be over-cautious, but because pneumonia at your age can turn serious quickly and home antibiotics might not be safe."

"I know hospital’s the last place you want to be. But the muddle is a warning sign I can’t ignore, and a few days getting the right treatment and oxygen could make all the difference. I’ll make the process as smooth as I can."

"They’ll start the right antibiotics for the severity. And once you’re through this, because you used to smoke, I want a follow-up chest X-ray in about six weeks to be sure it’s cleared completely — occasionally an infection sits on top of something we need to catch."

"If before you’re seen you become more breathless, drowsier, your lips go blue, or you can’t keep fluids down — call 999. And if you ever cough up blood or lose weight later, tell me. Let’s get you assessed properly today."

f.learning: Suspected COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED PNEUMONIA is a SEVERITY/DISPOSITION decision (home vs hospital), not a reflex prescription. Assess with CRB-65 — one point each for new CONFUSION, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, low Blood pressure (systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60), and age ≥65 — where higher scores indicate higher mortality risk and favour hospital assessment (NICE NG250 1.2.3: 0 usually primary care, 1 primary care with safety-netting or other community options, ≥2 consider hospital referral; in hospital CURB-65 adds Urea). CRB-65 is a guide, not the whole decision: also weigh oxygen saturations/oxygenation, respiratory rate and work of breathing, observations/NEWS, comorbidity (e.g. COPD), hydration, social support and ability to cope, and sepsis features — new confusion, hypoxia, tachypnoea, hypotension or significant comorbidity all lower the threshold to ADMIT. Recognise severe pneumonia/sepsis markers warranting admission (new confusion, RR ≥30, hypotension, low sats, age ≥65 with comorbidity, sepsis signs, inability to manage at home); an older COPD patient with new confusion and breathlessness is not a "carry on at home" case and needs face-to-face assessment of observations/sats and probable admission. Treat per severity/local guidance (antibiotics chosen by severity, antipyretics, fluids, oxygen if needed). Crucially, in an older EX-SMOKER arrange a follow-up CHEST X-RAY (~6 weeks) to confirm radiological resolution, because a non-resolving or recurrent same-site consolidation can hide an underlying LUNG CANCER (BTS 2009 and the NICE NG250 committee discussion support the ~6-week film for higher-risk people such as smokers; NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026): consider an urgent CXR at 40+ with persistent or recurrent chest infection, and offer one at 40+ to an ever-smoker with an unexplained symptom such as cough, breathlessness, chest pain or weight loss) — don’t let "just a chest infection" mask a tumour. The hidden agenda is minimisation and fear of hospital; assess severity properly, make the disposition decision out loud, address the hospital fear with empathy, assess his capacity to refuse admission if he declines (new confusion; Mental Capacity Act 2005), treat new confusion with infection as a sepsis warning sign (NICE NG253), arrange the resolution safety-net, and safety-net deterioration — not collude with antibiotics-and-carry-on.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG250 Pneumonia: diagnosis and management (2025) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over (2025) · [3] NICE NG115 COPD in over 16s · [5] British Thoracic Society guideline for the management of community acquired pneumonia in adults (2009) · [6] Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice
knowledge.summary: Cough, fever, pleuritic pain and breathlessness in a 71-year-old with COPD who is newly confused is suspected pneumonia with a CRB65 score of at least 2 before respiratory rate or blood pressure are even measured. NICE NG250 (1.2.3) says consider hospital referral at a score of 2 or more and refer if sepsis or cardiorespiratory failure is suspected; new confusion also needs sepsis assessment (NG253). The skill is making and explaining that disposition decision kindly, checking he can weigh it up, and planning a follow-up chest X-ray because he is an older ex-smoker.

points.t: NICE NG250 [1]: one point each for confusion (AMT 8 or less, or new disorientation in person, place or time), respiratory rate 30 or more a minute, blood pressure systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 or less, and age 65 or over. Use it with clinical judgement, bearing in mind comorbidities.

NICE NG250 [1]: score 0, primary care with safety-netting; score 1, primary care with safety-netting or referral to a virtual ward, same-day emergency care, hospital at home or hospital; score 2 or more, consider hospital referral. Refer anyone with signs of a more serious illness such as sepsis or cardiorespiratory failure.

NICE NG253 [2]: in a person with suspected infection, new confusion or altered mental state is a warning sign. Assess face to face with full observations (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, level of consciousness) against the NG253 risk criteria, with NEWS2 as an adjunct where locally adopted (NG253 applies it in acute hospital and ambulance settings); high-risk findings need emergency transfer.

Underlying COPD reduces reserve and makes hypoxia more likely. Hospital teams target oxygen saturations of 88 to 92% in people at risk of hypercapnia. NICE NG115 [3] covers exacerbation management if this proves to be an exacerbation rather than pneumonia.

NICE NG250 [1]: low-severity community-acquired pneumonia is treated with amoxicillin for 5 days (dose per BNF), with alternatives for penicillin allergy. Moderate and high severity is treated per NG250 and local guidance, usually in hospital. Do not delay transfer to start oral antibiotics at home if he needs admission.

NICE NG250 [1] does not support routine follow-up X-rays for everyone, but the committee noted their value for people at higher risk of lung cancer such as smokers and those over 50. BTS 2009 [5] advises a chest X-ray at about 6 weeks for persisting symptoms or signs or higher malignancy risk. NICE NG12 [4]: consider an urgent chest X-ray in people aged 40 and over with persistent or recurrent chest infection, and offer one to people aged 40 and over with 2 or more unexplained symptoms from cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss and appetite loss, or 1 or more if they have ever smoked.

A confused patient refusing admission needs a decision-specific capacity assessment (Mental Capacity Act 2005 [6]): can he understand, retain and weigh the information and communicate a choice? If he has capacity, respect the decision, make the best alternative plan and document. If not, act in his best interests, involving his wife.

ro.d: Picked up “the wife says I’ve been muddled” and explored it with a collateral history and orientation check.
Idea (just a chest infection), concern (going into hospital and not coming out the same), expectation (oral antibiotics at home).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror of hospital since his brother died there; wants his own bed. He doesn't recognise how muddled he is — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Halloran, I’m Dr Singh. I can see you’re not feeling great. Tell me what’s been happening.

It’s just a chest infection, doctor. Cough, bringing up green stuff, bit of a fever and my chest hurts when I breathe in. The wife says I’ve been a bit muddled. Can you just call in some antibiotics so I can fight it off at home? I don’t want to be sent into hospital.
I hear that you want to stay at home, and I’ll keep that in mind. Can I ask some questions first, and perhaps speak to your wife as well, so we get the plan right?
model.why: Acknowledges his wish and agrees the agenda, including a collateral history

model.text: Go on then. She’s here.
How long has this been going on, and how is your breathing compared with your usual COPD?
Four days. Breathing’s worse than normal. I’m puffed just getting to the loo.
Mrs Halloran, what have you noticed about him being muddled?
(Wife) He’s not himself. He got the day wrong this morning and he keeps repeating things. That’s not like him.
Thank you. Mr Halloran, do you know what day it is today, and where you are?
model.why: Brief orientation check for CRB65 confusion

model.text: (pause) Tuesday? No… I’m not sure. I’m at home.
That’s okay. Have you coughed up any blood? Any shivering fits, dizziness when you stand, or passing much less urine?
No blood. I’ve been shivery. Not been to the loo much.
Are you managing to drink? And have you used any extra inhalers or a rescue pack for your chest?
model.why: Hydration and COPD treatment so far

model.text: Not drinking much. Just my usual inhalers.
Do you have anything at home to check your oxygen or blood pressure? And any allergies to antibiotics?
No, nothing like that. No allergies.
You said you don’t want to go into hospital. Can you tell me what worries you about that?
model.why: Explores the fear behind the refusal

model.text: You go in and you don’t come out the same. I want my own bed.
That’s a very understandable fear, and I’m glad you told me. I want to be honest with you about what I’m seeing.
model.why: Validates the fear and signals honesty

model.text: With the cough, fever and pain on breathing, I think you may have pneumonia, an infection deeper in the lung. We use a score to judge how serious it is. You score a point for being over 65, and another for the new muddle. That already puts you in the group where we usually want hospital assessment, and I can’t measure your breathing rate, blood pressure or oxygen over video.
model.why: Explains suspected pneumonia and CRB65 out loud (NICE NG250)

model.text: It’s only a bit of confusion.

In someone your age, new confusion with an infection can mean the infection is affecting the whole body, which we call sepsis. Along with your COPD, being more breathless and not passing much water, that worries me. Antibiotic tablets at home may not be enough or quick enough.
model.why: Sepsis lens (NICE NG253), COPD and hydration inform disposition

model.text: So you want me to go in.

I do. I’d like the hospital team to check your oxygen and blood pressure, do a chest X-ray and bloods, and start the right antibiotics, possibly into a vein, and oxygen if you need it. With the confusion and breathlessness I’ll arrange an ambulance rather than you going by car. Many people with pneumonia go home within a few days once it’s under control. Could you tell me in your own words why I’m suggesting hospital?
model.why: Clear disposition with rationale; begins a capacity check

model.text: Because I might have pneumonia, and with the muddle and my chest it could get worse quickly at home.
That’s exactly it. What do you think about going?
model.why: Checks he can weigh the information and invites his decision

model.text: (to wife) What do you think? … All right. If it gets me home sooner.

Thank you, I know that wasn’t easy. I’ll ring the ambulance and send the hospital a summary now. Mrs Halloran, please pack his inhalers and a list of his medicines. Is someone able to be with you both?
model.why: Practical support and involves his wife

model.text: (Wife) I’ll go with him.
While you wait, sit him upright and give sips of water. If he gets much more breathless, drowsy or hard to wake, his lips go blue, or he collapses, call 999 straight away and say it’s urgent.
(Wife) Okay.

One more thing for later. Because you used to smoke, once you’ve recovered I’d like a repeat chest X-ray in about six weeks to make sure it has fully cleared. Sometimes an infection hides something else in the lung, and we want to be sure. If you ever cough up blood or lose weight, tell me. I’ll check in with you after you’re discharged.
model.why: Follow-up chest X-ray and review (NICE NG250, BTS, NICE NG12)

social.t: Older people often fear losing independence in hospital. Name it, explain the aim is to get him home safely, and involve his wife.
His wife is carrying worry and practical tasks. Check she has support and knows the plan.

legal.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: capacity is presumed but must be assessed when there is reason to doubt it, such as new confusion. The test is decision-specific. If he lacks capacity and refuses, act in his best interests, consulting his wife.
Record the CRB65 elements, the confusion history, the options discussed, his decision and the capacity assessment.

professional.t: Video cannot measure respiratory rate, saturations or blood pressure reliably. If the decision depends on them, arrange face-to-face or hospital assessment.
Send a clear summary to the admitting team with the history, CRB65, COPD and allergy status.

community.t: Community respiratory or virtual ward teams can support early discharge. Offer pneumococcal and seasonal vaccines per the Green Book once recovered, and pulmonary rehabilitation for COPD if appropriate.

redFlags: Breathlessness at rest or much worse than baseline
psychosocial: Fear of hospital and losing independence
ice: Idea: just a chest infection needing tablets
Concern: going into hospital and not coming out the same
Expectation: oral antibiotics and to stay at home

playbook.diagnosis: “I think you may have pneumonia, and because you’re newly confused and over 65, it scores as serious enough that you need checking in hospital today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Pneumonia is an infection deep in the small air sacs of the lung, so less oxygen gets into your blood. When the infection makes someone muddled, it’s a sign it’s affecting the whole body, not just the chest.”

management.reflectIce: “You want your own bed, and I want you back in it as soon as possible. Getting the right treatment today is the fastest way to do that.”
management.psychosocial: Name the fear of hospital; involve his wife; check his understanding and reasoning to support a capacitous decision.
sharedPlan: Hospital assessment by ambulance: CRB65 2 or more (NICE NG250) and sepsis concern (NICE NG253)
Observations, NEWS2, chest X-ray, bloods; antibiotics by severity; oxygen targets for COPD
Follow-up chest X-ray at about 6 weeks as an older ex-smoker (BTS 2009; NICE NG250)
safetyNet: Worse breathing, drowsiness, blue lips or collapse while waiting: 999
Haemoptysis or weight loss later: tell the GP (NICE NG12)

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you let the patient’s framing (“just a chest infection”) override a severity assessment. The confusion is the cue most candidates underplay.

items.fail: Prescribing oral antibiotics by phone without a severity assessment.
items.why: New confusion and age 65 or over give CRB65 of at least 2: NICE NG250 (1.2.3) says consider hospital referral.
items.fix: Score CRB65 out loud and arrange hospital assessment.

items.why: New confusion with infection is a sepsis warning sign (NICE NG253).
items.fix: Take a collateral history and check orientation.

items.fail: Forgetting that video cannot measure the observations that decide the plan.
items.why: Respiratory rate, blood pressure and saturations are needed; guessing is unsafe.
items.fix: Arrange same-day face-to-face or hospital assessment.

items.fail: No follow-up chest X-ray plan for an older ex-smoker.
items.why: Non-resolving consolidation can hide lung cancer (NICE NG250 committee discussion; BTS 2009; NICE NG12).
items.fix: Plan a chest X-ray at about 6 weeks and review.

items.fail: Overriding his refusal without exploring it, or colluding with it.
items.why: Both fail the patient. Capacity must be considered when a confused patient refuses.
items.fix: Explore the fear, explain, ask him to reason it back, and document.

items.fail: No safety-net while he waits for transport.
items.fix: Tell his wife exactly when to call 999.

Duration, breathlessness against baseline, collateral history of confusion, orientation, rigors, urine output, fluids, haemoptysis, allergies.
Fear of hospital and of not coming home the same. Name it.
Suspected pneumonia; CRB65 out loud; sepsis concern; why video cannot measure what matters.
Hospital by ambulance; check his reasoning; wife’s support; safety-net while waiting; 6-week chest X-ray; review.

wordPics.pass: Recognises suspected pneumonia, uses CRB65, identifies new confusion and age as reasons for hospital assessment, arranges it, and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: takes a collateral history and checks orientation; states the CRB65 score and sepsis concern out loud; weighs COPD and hydration; explores the fear of hospital; checks he can understand and weigh the decision; arranges an ambulance with a handover; plans the 6-week chest X-ray as an ex-smoker.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send some amoxicillin to the chemist. Carry on at home.”
avoid.instead: “With new muddle and worse breathing, I need your oxygen and blood pressure checked today in hospital.”
avoid.why: CRB65 of 2 or more with possible sepsis needs hospital assessment (NICE NG250, NG253).

avoid.dont: “You have to go in, there’s no choice.”
avoid.instead: “Can you tell me in your own words why I’m suggesting hospital? What do you think?”
avoid.why: Coercion damages trust; a capacity-respecting conversation usually reaches agreement.

Sometimes an infection hides something else in the lung, and we want to be sure. If you ever cough up blood or lose weight, tell me. I’ll check in with you after you’re discharged.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG250 Pneumonia: diagnosis and management (2025) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over (2025) · [3] NICE NG115 COPD in over 16s · [5] British Thoracic Society guideline for the management of community acquired pneumonia in adults (2009) · [6] Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Cough, fever, pleuritic pain and breathlessness in a 71-year-old with COPD who is newly confused is suspected pneumonia with a CRB65 score of at least 2 before respiratory rate or blood pressure are even measured. NICE NG250 (1.2.3) says consider hospital referral at a score of 2 or more and refer if sepsis or cardiorespiratory failure is suspected; new confusion also needs sepsis assessment (NG253). The skill is making and explaining that disposition decision kindly, checking he can weigh it up, and planning a follow-up chest X-ray because he is an older ex-smoker.

points.t: NICE NG250 [1]: one point each for confusion (AMT 8 or less, or new disorientation in person, place or time), respiratory rate 30 or more a minute, blood pressure systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 or less, and age 65 or over. Use it with clinical judgement, bearing in mind comorbidities.

NICE NG250 [1]: score 0, primary care with safety-netting; score 1, primary care with safety-netting or referral to a virtual ward, same-day emergency care, hospital at home or hospital; score 2 or more, consider hospital referral. Refer anyone with signs of a more serious illness such as sepsis or cardiorespiratory failure.

NICE NG253 [2]: in a person with suspected infection, new confusion or altered mental state is a warning sign. Assess face to face with full observations (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, level of consciousness) against the NG253 risk criteria, with NEWS2 as an adjunct where locally adopted (NG253 applies it in acute hospital and ambulance settings); high-risk findings need emergency transfer.

Underlying COPD reduces reserve and makes hypoxia more likely. Hospital teams target oxygen saturations of 88 to 92% in people at risk of hypercapnia. NICE NG115 [3] covers exacerbation management if this proves to be an exacerbation rather than pneumonia.

NICE NG250 [1]: low-severity community-acquired pneumonia is treated with amoxicillin for 5 days (dose per BNF), with alternatives for penicillin allergy. Moderate and high severity is treated per NG250 and local guidance, usually in hospital. Do not delay transfer to start oral antibiotics at home if he needs admission.

NICE NG250 [1] does not support routine follow-up X-rays for everyone, but the committee noted their value for people at higher risk of lung cancer such as smokers and those over 50. BTS 2009 [5] advises a chest X-ray at about 6 weeks for persisting symptoms or signs or higher malignancy risk. NICE NG12 [4]: consider an urgent chest X-ray in people aged 40 and over with persistent or recurrent chest infection, and offer one to people aged 40 and over with 2 or more unexplained symptoms from cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss and appetite loss, or 1 or more if they have ever smoked.

A confused patient refusing admission needs a decision-specific capacity assessment (Mental Capacity Act 2005 [6]): can he understand, retain and weigh the information and communicate a choice? If he has capacity, respect the decision, make the best alternative plan and document. If not, act in his best interests, involving his wife.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; acknowledged his wish to stay at home before exploring.
Wife’s observations, fear of hospital, fluid intake, who can support him.
Picked up “the wife says I’ve been muddled” and explored it with a collateral history and orientation check.
Idea (just a chest infection), concern (going into hospital and not coming out the same), expectation (oral antibiotics at home).
Recognised that respiratory rate, BP and saturations cannot be measured on video; hospital assessment with observations, NEWS2, chest X-ray and bloods.
Pneumonia versus COPD exacerbation; sepsis; older ex-smoker so underlying lung cancer in mind.
New confusion, breathlessness beyond baseline, rigors, reduced urine and haemoptysis screened.
Named suspected pneumonia with CRB65 of at least 2 (new confusion, age 65 or over) and a sepsis concern.
Hospital referral by ambulance (NICE NG250 1.2.3: CRB65 2 or more; NICE NG253 sepsis assessment); no delay for oral antibiotics.
COPD taken into account; his fear addressed; capacity to decide checked through teach-back and his reasoning; wife involved.
Safety-net while waiting; follow-up chest X-ray at about 6 weeks as an ex-smoker; review after discharge.

social.t: Older people often fear losing independence in hospital. Name it, explain the aim is to get him home safely, and involve his wife.
His wife is carrying worry and practical tasks. Check she has support and knows the plan.

legal.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: capacity is presumed but must be assessed when there is reason to doubt it, such as new confusion. The test is decision-specific. If he lacks capacity and refuses, act in his best interests, consulting his wife.
Record the CRB65 elements, the confusion history, the options discussed, his decision and the capacity assessment.

professional.t: Video cannot measure respiratory rate, saturations or blood pressure reliably. If the decision depends on them, arrange face-to-face or hospital assessment.
Send a clear summary to the admitting team with the history, CRB65, COPD and allergy status.

community.t: Community respiratory or virtual ward teams can support early discharge. Offer pneumococcal and seasonal vaccines per the Green Book once recovered, and pulmonary rehabilitation for COPD if appropriate.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you let the patient’s framing (“just a chest infection”) override a severity assessment. The confusion is the cue most candidates underplay.

items.fail: Prescribing oral antibiotics by phone without a severity assessment.
items.why: New confusion and age 65 or over give CRB65 of at least 2: NICE NG250 (1.2.3) says consider hospital referral.
items.fix: Score CRB65 out loud and arrange hospital assessment.

items.why: New confusion with infection is a sepsis warning sign (NICE NG253).
items.fix: Take a collateral history and check orientation.

items.fail: Forgetting that video cannot measure the observations that decide the plan.
items.why: Respiratory rate, blood pressure and saturations are needed; guessing is unsafe.
items.fix: Arrange same-day face-to-face or hospital assessment.

items.fail: No follow-up chest X-ray plan for an older ex-smoker.
items.why: Non-resolving consolidation can hide lung cancer (NICE NG250 committee discussion; BTS 2009; NICE NG12).
items.fix: Plan a chest X-ray at about 6 weeks and review.

items.fail: Overriding his refusal without exploring it, or colluding with it.
items.why: Both fail the patient. Capacity must be considered when a confused patient refuses.
items.fix: Explore the fear, explain, ask him to reason it back, and document.

items.fail: No safety-net while he waits for transport.
items.fix: Tell his wife exactly when to call 999.
